source_text: Sed tamen ille, qui fulmine tam perspicuae veritatis interiit, ex parte aliqua videtur spirare, cum confertur tibi; illi enim tota dogmatis sui fundamento eius tantummodo nutante structura collabitur, tibi autem tria similiter vacillant ut illi unum. Ac per hoc vide, utrum aedificii tui quidquam possit assurgere. Mani ergo putans naturale esse peccatum, quod nisi voluntarium esse non potest, in vacuo fundamenta locavit; reliqua vero iuxta se consequenter imposuit dicens, quoniam est naturale peccatum, malam esse naturam, malae autem rei auctorem bonum non esse ac per hoc omne humanum genus reputandum principi tenebrarum. Quod totum utique stare potuisset, nisi illud primum eius suffodisset veritas, id est peccatum opus liberae voluntatis doceri naturale non posse et, quidquid fuisset naturale, peccatum esse non posse.
pass_a_gloss: But nevertheless he who has perished by the thunderbolt of so clear a truth seems from some part to breathe, when he is conferred to you; for to him the whole structure of his dogma collapses with its foundation only nodding, but to you three similarly vacillate as to him one. And through this see whether anything of your building can rise. Mani therefore thinking sin to be natural, which unless voluntary cannot be, placed foundations in the empty; but the remaining he consequently imposed beside themselves saying, since there is natural sin, nature is evil, but the author of an evil thing is not good, and through this the whole human race is to be reputated to the prince of darkness. Which whole indeed could have stood, unless truth had undermined that first of his, that is that sin a work of free will cannot be taught natural and whatever had been natural cannot be sin.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: Yet the man slain by the thunderbolt of such clear truth seems still to breathe in some respect when compared with you. His whole doctrinal structure collapses when only its foundation gives way. But three things in your case totter as his one does. Consider, then, whether any part of your building can rise.

Mani thought sin natural, though it can only be voluntary, and so laid his foundations in empty space. The rest he placed consistently alongside: since sin is natural, nature is evil; an evil thing cannot have a good author; therefore the whole human race must be attributed to the prince of darkness. All this could have stood, had truth not undermined his first claim: sin, a work of free will, cannot be shown natural, and whatever is natural cannot be sin.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
